issues.legal_issue: A High Court should ordinarily not entertain a writ petition challenging a recovery tribunal’s order when an effective statutory appeal is available and has not been exhausted.
material_facts: The borrowers challenged the recovery tribunal’s order in the High Court under Article 226 without pursuing the available appeal to the appellate tribunal.
The tribunal’s order was appealable, subject to a pre-deposit requirement, and the borrowers gave no reasonable justification for bypassing that remedy.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the writ petition without the borrowers first exhausting the available statutory appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, the rule requiring exhaustion of an effective alternative remedy is one of discretion, not compulsion. But in recovery matters involving public dues and financial institutions, the High Court should ordinarily insist that the remedies provided by the relevant statute be exhausted. The Court relied on United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tondon, (2010) 8 SCC 110, and observed that bypassing the appeal appeared to avoid the pre-deposit condition under the second proviso to Section 18 of the SARFAESI Act, 2002.

rule.if: recovery_action_challenge and appealable_tribunal_order and effective_statutory_appeal_available and appeal_not_exhausted and no_reasonable_bypass_justification

predicates.recovery_action_challenge: A person challenged a tribunal order concerning a financial institution’s recovery action.
predicates.appealable_tribunal_order: The tribunal order could be challenged through a statutory appeal.
predicates.effective_statutory_appeal_available: The statutory appeal provided an available remedy for the grievance.
predicates.appeal_not_exhausted: The challenger filed a writ petition without first pursuing the statutory appeal.
predicates.no_reasonable_bypass_justification: The challenger gave no reasonable justification for bypassing the available appeal.

issues.definition: When a recovery-action challenge concerns an appealable tribunal order, an effective appeal remains unused, and no reasonable justification for bypassing it is given, the High Court should not entertain the writ petition.

issues.legal_issue: An inadvertent error in a property identifier does not invalidate a secured-property auction when the property is otherwise unambiguously described and no prejudice is shown.
material_facts: The property identifier in the recovery and auction notices contained an inadvertent typographical error.
The notices also gave the property’s measurements, boundaries, and other identifying details, which were sufficient to identify it.

No other property with the erroneous identifier existed in the locality, and the borrowers did not show that bidders were misled, that the property was ambiguous, or that the error caused a loss in value.
issues.conclusion: The typographical error was inconsequential and did not vitiate the auction proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: A secured creditor is obliged to check the description of the mortgaged property in the initial and subsequent proceedings. However, an inadvertent error that causes no demonstrated prejudice does not, by itself, justify annulling an otherwise compliant process. Where the property’s detailed description is unambiguous, a typographical error in its identifier does not vitiate the auction under the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002.

rule.if: secured_property_e_auction_challenge and inadvertent_identifier_error and complete_identifying_details and no_competing_property_with_error_identifier and no_prejudice_demonstrated

predicates.secured_property_e_auction_challenge: A challenge was made to an auction of property offered as security for a debt.
predicates.inadvertent_identifier_error: The property identifier contained an inadvertent typographical error.
predicates.complete_identifying_details: The auction materials included other details sufficient to identify the property unambiguously.
predicates.no_competing_property_with_error_identif: No other property in the locality had the erroneous identifier.
predicates.no_prejudice_demonstrated: The borrowers did not establish that the error misled participants, caused ambiguity, or reduced the property’s sale value.

issues.definition: If a secured-property auction is challenged over an inadvertent identifier error, but other details unambiguously identify the property, no competing property has that identifier, and no prejudice is demonstrated, the error does not invalidate the auction.

issues.legal_issue: A short delay in paying the balance of an auction price does not invalidate the sale when the delay arises from the circumstances of pending proceedings and the borrowers’ conduct, rather than a default by the purchaser.
material_facts: The auction purchaser paid the initial portion of the bid and deposited the balance four days after the stated deadline.
The tribunal had permitted the auction to proceed subject to the borrowers making a deposit, but the borrowers sought further time and did not make that deposit.

The bank asked the purchaser to wait while the borrowers negotiated with it in light of the tribunal proceedings; the purchaser paid the balance while the matter remained in flux, and the auction was not stayed.
The applicable pre-amendment rule allowed the payment period to be extended by agreement in writing, and the later amendment to the rule did not apply to this auction.
issues.conclusion: In these circumstances, the four-day delay did not frustrate or annul the auction proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under the pre-amendment Rule 9(4) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002, the fifteen-day payment period was not absolute and could be extended by written agreement. In General Manager, Sri Siddeshwara Cooperative Bank Limited v. Ikbal, (2013) 10 SCC 83, the Court explained that the parties for this purpose included the secured creditor, borrower, and auction purchaser. Although the later amendment specified an agreement between the purchaser and secured creditor and imposed an outer limit, it did not govern this earlier auction. Considering the pending proceedings, the bank’s request that the purchaser wait, and the borrowers’ repeated failure to make the deposit required by the tribunal, the short delay did not justify setting aside the sale.

rule.if: secured_property_auction_payment_dispute and purchaser_paid_initial_share and brief_balance_payment_delay and auction_not_stayed and bank_requested_purchaser_to_wait and borrowers_sought_extensions and borrowers_failed_to_make_required_deposit

predicates.secured_property_auction_payment_dispute: A dispute concerned whether an auction sale was invalid because the purchaser paid the balance price late.
predicates.purchaser_paid_initial_share: The purchaser paid the initial portion of the auction price.
predicates.brief_balance_payment_delay: The purchaser paid the balance shortly after the stated deadline.
predicates.auction_not_stayed: The tribunal permitted the auction to proceed and did not stay it.
predicates.bank_requested_purchaser_to_wait: The secured creditor asked the purchaser to wait while the borrowers negotiated with it in light of the proceedings.
predicates.borrowers_sought_extensions: The borrowers sought additional time to meet a condition imposed in the pending proceedings.
predicates.borrowers_failed_to_make_required_deposi: The borrowers did not make the deposit required by the tribunal, including during the additional time granted.

issues.definition: When an auction-payment dispute involves a purchaser who paid the initial share but paid the balance only shortly late, the auction was not stayed, the creditor asked the purchaser to wait, and the borrowers sought extensions but failed to make the required deposit, the short delay does not invalidate the auction.
